analysis.one_liner: Exempts most drilling in units where federal minerals are a minority share from federal drilling permits.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Energy Committee and died at the end of the 113th Congress with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let oil and gas drilling proceed inside a drilling or spacing unit without a Bureau of Land Management drilling permit, as long as less than half the minerals in the unit are federally owned and the federal government neither owns nor leases the land surface there. Federal rights to royalty payments on federal minerals would be preserved. It would have shifted oversight of drilling activity touching federal minerals from federal regulators to state requirements alone.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas operators drilling in units that mix federal and private minerals would gain, because they could drill without obtaining a federal BLM drilling permit and would answer only to state rules. That would cut permitting time and cost for companies working in places like North Dakota's Bakken region, where split mineral ownership is common.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the requirement for a BLM drilling permit for any action within a drilling or spacing unit where less than 50% of minerals are federally owned and the federal government does not own or lease the surface [S2][S3].

Preserves the federal government's right to collect royalties on federal minerals produced from those units, so companies would still pay royalties but would not need federal drilling approval [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the cost of reduced federal oversight: BLM rules exist to prevent waste of federal minerals, protect against improper drilling practices, and verify that royalty payments are accurate. Where federal minerals sit under largely private units, drilling could proceed under state rules only, with federal regulators no longer reviewing the operations that draw on the government's mineral share.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal oversight and public mineral protection

drawbacks.text: Removing the federal permit requirement for actions touching federal minerals would leave royalty collection, waste prevention, and drilling practices on those federal minerals to state regulation alone [S2][S3].

The bill covers units where the federal government owns a substantial minority share of minerals (up to just under 50%), so a meaningful amount of publicly owned minerals could be produced with no federal operational review [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is faster, cheaper permitting for drilling companies in mixed-ownership units. The cost is that federal minerals — which belong to the public — could be produced with no federal review of how they are drilled or whether royalties are computed correctly. The bill preserves royalty payments but removes the oversight that protects the public's share, so the trade favors operators over the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee in September 2014, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Hoeven introduced the bill on September 18, 2014, late in the second session of the 113th Congress [S1][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, where it stayed [S5].
No committee markup, floor vote, or further action occurred before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public's current federal oversight of drilling on federal minerals stayed in place, since the bill never advanced; drilling operators remain subject to the federal permitting they sought to avoid.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal regulators and public mineral oversight

for.name: Sen. John Hoeven
for.role: U.S. Senator from North Dakota (bill sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt mixed-ownership drilling units from BLM permitting

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote, no report before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no committee or floor action, so no partisan split is visible in the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: Operators in units with minority federal mineral ownership could drill without a federal BLM permit, cutting permitting time and cost. The gain comes at the expense of federal oversight of operations that produce publicly owned minerals.

industries.industry: Federal government (treasury and Bureau of Land Management)
industries.note: BLM would lose permit authority over drilling actions touching federal minerals in mixed-ownership units, weakening its ability to prevent waste and verify royalty accuracy, though royalty payments themselves would continue.
